summary: Fieldstone tower on Mount Prospect in Weeks State Park, Lancaster NH; built 1912 as a private observation and water tower; enclosed state cab added after 1941; still active.

facts.design: Split fieldstone tower with a round, enclosed lookout cab added by the state after 1941

access.note: Inside Weeks State Park. Museum, tower and auto road open Memorial Day weekend to Columbus Day; visitors are invited to climb the 48 steps (2026 state information sheet).

visit.trail_note: Scenic drive up the Mountain Road to the summit; the park also has trails. The 2026 information sheet lists climbing the stone tower as a visitor activity.

facts.agency: NH Dept. of Resources and Economic Development

events.note: Built by John Wingate Weeks as an observation and water tower for his summer estate; estate construction finished in 1912
Weeks died; he left the estate to his children

Children donated the estate to the State of New Hampshire, which became a state park. The Register says the state then added a round enclosed lookout cab; the 2026 information sheet says the tower was converted after 1941 to include a fire lookout.
Registered August 8, 1992 as US 43, NH 2; nominated by Stephen J. Cummings and Mark W. MacDonald

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The Register ties the enclosed cab to 1941, when the estate became a state park. The 2026 state information sheet says the tower was converted after 1941 to include a fire lookout. The story reports both dates and does not choose between them.
The historic-structures summary gives 37 feet for the 1912 observation and water tower. No current height appears in the readable sources, so no height_m is recorded.

sources.title: Mount Prospect Fire Tower, Lancaster New Hampshire
Weeks State Park and the John Wingate Weeks Historic Site, 2026 information sheet

notes_for_editor: Core history (1912 estate tower, 1941 transfer to the state, enclosed cab, 1992 registration) is consistent across the Register, the historic-structures summary and the 2026 state sheet. Open points: whether the cab came in 1941 or after; current height (37 ft in one summary; a Weeks State Park Association search snippet says 56 ft, not fetched so not used); staffing is not stated. The historic-structures page gives 420 acres for the estate in one place and donated 431 acres in another; the story avoids acreage. The NH Division of Forests and Lands history PDF returned HTTP 403, so it was not used.
